name: Soong May-ling
role: Republic of China first lady, wartime diplomat and Nationalist advocate
summary: Soong advocated international cooperation against aggression, Chinese national reconstruction and a public role for Christian social service. Her speeches praised parliamentary consent and women’s civic rights, while she emphasized national duty and later campaigned for Nationalist recovery of mainland China.

notes:
Reviewed wartime speeches, New Life essays, women’s constitutional debates and Taiwan-era biography. Her public constitutional ideals are distinguished from the authoritarian practice of the government she represented; no position is assigned solely from her husband’s actions. No specific economic system, reproductive policy or modern ecological position was established. No inferred answers.

Merged with an independent claude-sonnet-5-5 audit: 55 answers taken from it, 16 agreed, 0 conflicts settled by the integrator.

claude-sonnet-5-5 notes: Independent second pass (claude-sonnet-5-5) using her own text in full: We Chinese Women (1942, incl. the Atlantic article), her three 1943 US speeches in The Voice of China, My Religion (1934) and The Sure Victory (1955). The pamphlet 'Outline of the New Life Movement' on archive.org is her husband's text (she only translated it) and was not used. Her views as stated: Sun Yat-sen's three principles, a Chinese socialism without communism, state-owned utilities, progressive taxation, merit-based civil service, a strong international order, no imperialism. Where she opposed permanent one-party rule in 1942 she was herself part of the Kuomintang's party state, so one-party-rule is 0 low and suppress-opposition is low. Her husband's speeches in the same book were not used. Themes searched: economy, government, society, world, liberty, culture, ecology (nothing), technology (nothing), means, globalism. Britannica was behind a Cloudflare wall and not used. No ecological, technology, reproductive-rights, criminal-justice or sexuality positions were found. 'China Shall Rise Again' and 'This Is Our China' are lending-only on archive.org (401/404 on the text file) and were not read.
